All three use the same planar coordinates, but they describe different relationships. The dial center is the origin. Positive x points right, and positive y points down in SVG screen coordinates. Negative coordinates are normal: the upper half of a centered dial has negative y values. The view box determines which rectangle of that coordinate plane appears on the page; it does not move the origin to the upper-left corner of the dial. Polar placement uses the ordinary formulas x = d\cos\theta, \qquad y = d\sin\theta. Thus zero radians points right, \pi/2 points down, \pi points left, and -\pi/2 points up. Increasing a polar angle appears clockwise on screen because y increases downward. Importing the coordinates into a program that displays positive y upward can mirror that apparent orientation unless the receiving coordinate convention is accounted for. Placement angles and most geometric phase or grid-rotation values are in radians. There are specific exceptions: a V-bit’s included angle and cube’s leg_angle are in degrees. Paon’s fan_angle is a phase-envelope scale, despite its name. There is no universal angle unit that can safely be inferred from the word “angle.”

s: Clock positions follow the hour hand
x: Clock placement describes the direction of the hour hand, including its movement between hours. The helper converts an hour h and minute m to \theta = -\frac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi\frac{60(h\bmod 12)+m}{720}. The full turn is 12 hours, or 720 minutes. At distance d, 12:00 is (0,-d), 3:00 is (d,0), 6:00 is (0,d), and 9:00 is (-d,0). At 3:30 the center lies halfway between the 3 and 4 hour positions, 15 degrees clockwise from 3:00. It does not point to 6 as the minute hand would. Similarly, 12:30 is only 15 degrees clockwise from the top. The clock direction and distance determine the layer’s center. A distance of zero leaves that center at the origin regardless of the hour. The layer’s own radius determines its size around that center; it is not another way to specify the distance from the dial center.

s: Translation does not reorient a motif
x: A layer generally computes its motif around a local center and adds center_x and center_y to obtain drawing coordinates. Polar and clock constructors calculate those offsets; they do not automatically rotate the motif to face outward or scale it to fit the remaining space. For example, moving a clous de Paris layer toward 3:00 leaves the grid’s configured rotation unchanged. Moving a paon layer leaves its fan orientation unchanged. The resulting composition can therefore place the same visual motif at several locations without turning each copy into a radial arrangement. The composition retains the independently generated paths. An offset motif can overlap a background, another motif, or the dial edge. The dial radius supplies a global boundary, but it does not resize the layer or create a separate circular mask around every displaced center.

s: Local and global boundaries solve different problems
x: There are two boundary levels. A local boundary belongs to a particular layer. Clous de Paris computes line endpoints on its own circle. Cube clips its zigzag segments to a local circle, then rotates and translates them. Paon retains samples inside its local circle, so its endpoints approximate the boundary at the selected sampling density rather than using the same analytic trimming as clous de Paris. Moving one of these layers moves its local region too. Not every family has such a local clipping step. Flinqué uses its radius to arrange the ring band but adds waves beyond the base radii. Limaçon can exceed its base radius, and draperie generates its configured ring band without clipping it to an enclosing dial. A size parameter is not automatically a clipping radius. The global boundary belongs to the combined dial. The watch-face and combined guilloché SVG exporters apply a circular clip path centered at the origin to the pattern group. A locally bounded layer can still cross this global boundary when offset. Conversely, a layer without a local clip can be visibly trimmed by the global dial circle. Geometry and exports Why does a convincing dial preview not imply a machinable solid? Turtles primarily generates ordered paths. Exporters translate those paths into drawing commands, CAD curves, or triangles, but each translation retains only part of the design model. The format’s ability to describe a solid does not mean the exporter constructs one. The common object is a path Direct layers store sampled coordinates in ordered lists. The combined composition gathers every supported family into a collection of 2D paths. The exporters work from those samples, so smooth mathematical curves generally become straight segments between consecutive points. They are not automatically fitted to exact circles, splines, or CNC arcs. This representation preserves the trace of a motif without defining the material around it. Intersections between paths do not become joined CAD topology, and overlapping strokes do not cause a Boolean cut. Likewise, a closed loop is not automatically a filled region or a boundary of stock. Spherical spirographs expose an important difference between standalone and combined output. The standalone object retains both its planar trace and dome-projected 3D points.

s: A clipping mask is not trimmed geometry
x: The two boundary levels distinguish a layer’s own region from the global dial circle. At the global level, combined SVG hides pattern content outside a circular clip path. The source path coordinates can still extend beyond the circle; the viewer simply does not show that ink. Combined STEP and STL instead use geometrically clipped paths. The clipper intersects each sampled segment with the dial circle, inserts boundary points, and splits a path when it leaves and later reenters. It can also retain the portion of a crossing segment whose two endpoints are both outside. Keeping the pieces separate avoids adding a chord over the discarded interval. This trimming limits the path coordinates exported by those combined exporters. It does not remove the hidden coordinates from the original layer, enforce every family’s local boundary, or account for cutter width. A centerline ending on the dial edge can still put part of a finite-width tool beyond that edge. Standalone spirograph and single-lathe exports do not acquire the composition’s global dial clipping merely by using the same file format.

The implemented STEP writer emits an ISO 10303-21 file using the AP214 schema. It creates referenced Cartesian points, a POLYLINE for each path with at least two points, and a GEOMETRIC_CURVE_SET connected to the product’s shape representation. Its length unit is millimeters. This is CAD curve geometry. It contains no swept grooves, faces, shell, or boundary-representation solid. The writer retains the supplied vertices rather than converting an apparent circle into an analytic STEP circle. The representation’s numerical uncertainty declaration does not establish the approximation error between a sampled path and its original formula. For combined guilloché and watch-face output, all curves lie at z = 0 after global clipping. Standalone planar spirographs likewise become curves at z = 0; standalone spherical spirographs retain their generated z values. The working STEP adapters ignore the export configuration, so changing depth, base thickness, or tool radius does not give these curves a physical section or change their height. Pattern models Why can two turtles objects produce similar decoration but behave differently when inspected or exported? The answer depends on what each object models: a mathematical curve, an arrangement of curves, or a simplified sequence of engine passes. A family name describes a visual construction in this library; it does not establish that every implementation with that name represents the same machine motion. Direct layers describe the drawing A direct layer computes points from its geometry and stores them as one or more ordered paths. A spirograph follows one parameterized curve. Other families produce collections of rings, circles, figure-eights, or passes. The visible texture comes from the relationship between those paths, often without any surface model behind them. GuillochePattern collects the supported direct layer families and generates each independently. It retains their paths rather than merging intersections into a surface or subtracting one layer from another. Overlapping a small pattern with a background therefore adds lines; it does not reserve a blank subdial region. WatchFace wraps that composition with dial, bezel, and hole decorations for SVG. The horizontal spirograph uses a hypotrochoid: a point associated with a circle rolling inside a larger circle. The radius ratio sets the relative rolling motion, while the pen offset sets the size of the loops. In this implementation, point_distance is a fraction of the rolling circle’s radius, not an absolute distance in millimeters. Values above one put the pen outside that circle and can extend the curve beyond its nominal outer radius. The vertical variant adds a sinusoidal displacement to the y coordinate of the same base curve. “Vertical” describes an extra in-plane wave, not a second physical plane. The spherical variant retains the planar trace and also computes points on a dome. Its SVG uses the planar trace; its standalone 3D exports can retain dome height. That height is lost when the layer enters the combined composition’s 2D path collection. The number of rotations controls how far a spirograph is traced. It does not guarantee closure. Closure depends on the relationship between the rolling frequencies and the traced interval, so an unfinished trace can have separate endpoints even when it looks nearly periodic. Flinqué builds concentric rings with a repeated absolute-sine radial displacement. Each ring has pointed troughs, rounded peaks, and a smaller sinusoidal ripple. Petal count controls the main lobes around a ring; ring count controls how many traces fill the radial band. The ripple frequency affects detail along a trace, not the number of concentric rings. The nominal outer radius positions the ring band, but the added displacement can extend beyond it. Flinqué rings with radial petal structure Draperie uses concentric wavy rings whose peaks shift sideways as the radius changes. A single ring is a radial wave; the apparent fabric folds emerge from the alignment of many rings. Its base radius is the center of the ring band, not the innermost radius. With N rings and spacing s, ring i has nominal radius R_i = R_0 + \\left(i - \\frac{N-1}{2}\\right)s. The phase applied to that ring is an angular offset, multiplied by the wave frequency inside the radial sine. The cross-ring variation is \\phi_i = S,F\\left(\\frac{2\\pi C i}{N}\\right), where S is the phase-shift amplitude, C is the number of phase oscillations across the stack, and F controls the fold shape. Paon’s feather-like arches come from a fan of oscillating traces. The current generator places a vanishing point below the circle in SVG coordinates, spreads lines by angle, and adds horizontal oscillation. Oscillation phase varies logarithmically with distance from the vanishing point, so wavelengths grow toward the top of the image. A phase envelope across the fan creates the arch columns. This geometry differs from older comments describing parallel horizontal passes. Despite its name, fan_angle scales the cross-fan phase envelope in wave-cycle units; the fan’s geometric spread is computed from the circle and vanishing point. Additional Fourier harmonics sharpen the oscillation toward a triangle wave. The resulting density bands suggest feather edges without defining raised or recessed feather-shaped faces. s: Rose-engine simulation describes displacement and passes
x: The general rose-engine model starts with spindle angle. A rosette supplies radial displacement, scaled by amplitude and added to a base radius. A secondary rosette can add another displacement. RoseEngineLathe samples that radius over an angular interval and derives a tool centerline, approximate left and right cut edges, and optional depth and shading values. This is a geometric simulation of selected engine behavior. The cut edges are offsets by half the configured bit width along an estimated path normal. They are not a full sweep of the bit’s cross-section through stock, and they do not resolve overlapping cuts or self-intersections. RoseEngineLatheRun repeats passes. In its ordinary phase-rotation mode, each pass advances the primary rosette phase. With a nonzero radius step, it instead distributes base radii around the configured radius and can vary phase across that ring stack. The general run can also break traces into pieces with drawing gaps. Those gaps are a preview convention based on sampled point counts, not a planned retract-and-approach sequence. Named run constructors do not all follow this general simulation path. Limaçon uses the ordinary sinusoidal radial model

s: Sampling changes what can be seen
x: The exported paths approximate curves with straight segments. Resolution controls the samples along a path, while ring count, curve count, and pass count control how many paths exist. Adding curves increases pattern density; adding samples improves the representation of each curve. Those changes solve different problems. Uniform angular sampling is not uniform distance sampling on most modulated curves. Sharp corners, tight loops, high-frequency ripples, and additional harmonics can need more samples than broad smooth sections. If samples land at repeating phases of a wave, the sampled output can suppress or misrepresent that wave. This is geometric aliasing: detail is already absent or wrong in the stored points, before any image viewer draws it. A custom rosette’s lookup table introduces another sampling limit that a finer spindle-angle grid cannot fully undo. Resolution is not a universal quality control. Flinqué derives its angular sample count from petal count. Clous de Paris adds samples along already straight lines, so extra points do not reveal more curvature. s: Python and Rust share the geometry, not every interface
x: The Rust core implements the curve generation, composition, clipping, and exporters described here. The PyO3 extension wraps those types, translates arguments and errors, and presents point collections as Python tuples. The public Python package re-exports the extension classes and adds a convenience WatchFace wrapper. It is not a second Python implementation of the pattern mathematics. That shared core does not make the interfaces interchangeable. Rust commonly accepts configuration structs, while Python constructors and convenience methods collect scalar arguments. Some Rust settings or inspection methods are not exposed by the bindings. Python’s WatchFace also declares subdial and window helpers that currently raise NotImplementedError; an offset pattern layer is not the same feature as either helper. The pattern reference describes the direct interfaces, the composition reference describes how layers are collected, and the rose-engine reference distinguishes the simulation interfaces. Coordinates explains placement and boundaries; geometry and exports explains which parts of these models reach each output format.

How to export patterns Generate geometry before exporting, then choose the output for the next task: Use SVG to inspect paths, placement, and dial decorations. Use STEP to exchange sampled curves with CAD software where the exporter is implemented. Use STL to inspect the library’s approximate triangle ribbons, not to obtain a watertight dial or finished engraving. Use a direct layer’s or multi-pass run’s get_lines() to process sampled polylines yourself. These examples require an installed package. Every Python block is self-contained and writes only under the current working directory. Exporters take string filenames; convert a pathlib.Path with str(). s: Export one direct layer or retrieve its lines
x: For an isolated motif, use its own to_svg() and get_lines() methods. The returned value is a list of polylines, each containing (x, y) tuples in millimeters. Keep the lines separate when processing them; joining them would insert connecting segments that are not part of the pattern. import json from pathlib import Path from turtles import ClousDeParisLayer layer = ClousDeParisLayer(spacing=1.0, radius=10.0, resolution=2) layer.generate() layer.to_svg("standalone-layer.svg") lines = layer.get_lines() assert lines Path("standalone-lines.json").write_text(json.dumps(lines), encoding="utf-8") JSON represents the coordinate tuples as arrays. If you need STEP or STL for a direct layer, add it to a WatchFace and generate the face, as in the previous section. Direct layer classes do not have standalone to_step() or to_stl() methods. Use a face radius within its supported 26–44 mm range even if the layer itself is smaller.

All three standalone spirograph classes support SVG, STEP, and STL. Export a SphericalSpirograph directly if you need to retain its projected dome in STEP or STL: from turtles import SphericalSpirograph spirograph = SphericalSpirograph( outer_radius=12.0, radius_ratio=0.7, point_distance=0.8, rotations=7, resolution=120, dome_height=2.0, ) spirograph.generate() spirograph.to_svg("spherical-preview.svg") spirograph.to_step("spherical-curves.step", depth=0.1) spirograph.to_stl("spherical-ribbons.stl", depth=0.1, base_thickness=2.0) The SVG remains a planar preview. Standalone spirograph exports do not acquire the composition’s dial-boundary clipping. If standalone STL shows a straight connecting wall that SVG does not show, inspect the first and last samples: the standalone STL exporter connects the end back to the start even when the trace is incomplete. SVG and STEP do not force that closure. See geometry and exports before relying on a mesh’s apparent shape.

Configure the rosette and cutting bit before constructing RoseEngineLathe, then generate and export it. Its implemented file exporters are SVG and STL. from turtles import CuttingBit, RoseEngineConfig, RoseEngineLathe config = RoseEngineConfig.classic_multi_lobe( base_radius=12.0, lobes=8, amplitude=0.5, ) config.set_resolution(120) bit = CuttingBit.v_shaped(angle=60.0, width=0.3) lathe = RoseEngineLathe(config, bit) lathe.generate() lathe.to_svg("single-pass.svg") lathe.to_stl("single-pass.stl", depth=0.1, base_thickness=2.0) RoseEngineLathe.to_step() exists but currently raises OSError because STEP export is unimplemented. Its STL follows the centerline; the cutting bit’s width and the SVG’s approximate cut edges do not become a swept groove in that mesh. The single-lathe Python class does not expose get_lines().

s: Write all combined formats with one call
x: For a GuillochePattern, use export_all() with an extension-free base name. s: Check output before using it downstream
x: If an SVG contains decorations but no texture, call generate() after adding the layers. An ungenerated composition can still write SVG decorations; STL and STEP reject a composition without drawable paths after clipping. For an isolated layer or run, generate that original object rather than assuming that generating a composition also populated it. If export raises OSError, check the error message, generation state, destination directory, and write permissions. Invalid construction parameters normally raise ValueError instead. Refer to the error reference for the distinction; the unimplemented single-lathe STEP exporter is also reported as an export error. Before CAD exchange or manufacturing work: Confirm scale in the receiving application. SVG and STEP declare millimeters; STL contains coordinate values intended as millimeters but has no unit field. Inspect clipping, overlaps, endpoint connections, and sample density. Increase the relevant family’s sampling parameter before regenerating if its curves appear faceted; not every resolution argument changes generated vertices. Treat STEP as sampled polyline curves and STL as uncapped, zero-width ribbons. Neither output supplies finis

Install a stable Rust toolchain, including rustc and cargo, through rustup. Source builds also need the platform’s native linker and build tools. On macOS, install the Xcode Command Line Tools if the compiler reports a missing linker or SDK. With Git, Python 3.11 or newer, and Rust available: git clone https://github.com/1kbgz/turtles.git cd turtles python3.11 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install -e . After changing Rust code or bindings, repeat the editable installation to rebuild the extension, then restart any Python process that already imported it. For tests and documentation work, install the development and documentation extras from the repository root: python -m pip install -e '.[develop,docs]' Continue with the development guide for tests and build commands.

Use the nested Rust manifest for the Rust library crate named turtles. The repository-root manifest instead builds the Python extension package named turtles_py. To build the library from the repository root: cargo build --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml To consume it from another Rust project, add a path dependency to that project’s dependency table. Point it at the nested Rust crate, not the repository root. See the Rust reference for public types and the differences from the Python API.

If import turtles fails, check which interpreter owns the installation: python -m pip show pyturtles If the distribution is missing, activate the intended environment and reinstall it there. Rust methods do not automatically become methods of either Python class. Related reference: Patterns, Exports, Errors, Rose engine, and Rust API. Shared units, validation, and lifecycle Both constructors take a radius in millimeters, not a diameter. The radius must be finite and in [26, 44] mm inclusive. A radius of 38 mm produces a 76 mm diameter dial. This restriction belongs to the compositor; smaller standalone layers and spirographs are valid. Cartesian positions, center distances, pattern lengths, and export depths are in millimeters. Polar positioning and pattern rotations use radians; CubeLayer.leg_angle uses degrees. Paon’s fan_angle is a phase amplitude in wave cycles, not a geometric angle. Clock placement uses the hour hand, including the minute contribution, with 12:00 upward (negative y) and 3:00 rightward. WatchFace(radius: float) Creates an empty dial composition without an inner circle, bezel, center hole, or pattern layers. radius is the only public read-only property and returns the dial radius in mm. Its finite, inclusive 26–44 mm constraint is described above. The signatures below are bound-method calls: face denotes a WatchFace instance. They describe the public wrapper, not turtles.RustWatchFace or its internal _watch_face object.

Signature Effect face.add_inner() Enables the dial circle at face.radius, with fill #fafaf5, stroke #2c2c2c, and stroke width 0.3 mm. face.add_outer() Enables an unfilled bezel circle at 1.05 * face.radius, with stroke #1a1a1a and stroke width 0.8 mm. face.add_center_hole() Appends a filled #1a1a1a circle at the origin with radius 0.8 mm. face.add_hole(hour: int, minute: int, radius: float, hole_radius: float) Appends a filled #1a1a1a circle centered at the given clock position, radius mm from the dial center, with radius hole_radius mm. For add_hole(), radius means center distance, not hole size or dial size; hole_radius supplies the hole size. The implementation performs clock conversion but does not validate positive/finite hole size, positive/finite distance, or containment within the dial. Repeated add_inner() or add_outer() calls replace the corresponding configuration; repeated hole calls append more circles. These elements are SVG decorations. Combined STL and STEP delegate to the pattern compositor; they do not construct the inner disk, bezel solid, or physical hole cuts. The wrapper exposes no styling configuration arguments.

face.add_subdial(hour: int, minute: int, radius: float, subdial_radius: float) face.add_window(hour: int, minute: int, width: float, height: float, angle: float = 0.0) add_subdial() always raises NotImplementedError("add_subdial is not implemented yet"). add_window() always raises NotImplementedError("add_window is not implemented yet"). Neither renders, mutates the composition, nor validates its intended geometry. The intended window angle unit is degrees, but no rotation is implemented. Positioned texture layers do not implement these dial elements. add_hour_marks() and add_minute_marks() are not exposed methods.

It copies configuration and center into a fresh, ungenerated internal layer. add(layer) dispatches the eight standalone classes to those methods. Other objects are passed to the binding’s spirograph adder, which accepts only HorizontalSpirograph, VerticalSpirograph, or SphericalSpirograph; unsupported objects raise TypeError. add() does not accept a GuillochePattern, RoseEngineLathe, or RoseEngineLatheRun. The public wrapper has no add_layer(), add_layer_at_clock(), add_layer_at_polar(), or family-specific polar methods. Their presence in a Rust implementation or raw binding is not part of this wrapper’s API.

All methods below append one layer at the hour-hand center given by hour, minute, and distance. The default distance=0.0 centers the layer regardless of the clock position. None size defaults are resolved from face.radius before construction; explicit values retain the standalone family’s validation. Parameter meanings and units not repeated here match Patterns.

This radius is nominal ring size, not a local clipping boundary; composed export applies the dial boundary separately.

Amplitude is automatic and has no Python argument. add_draperie_sharp() calls add_draperie() with phase_exponent=1 and circular_phase=0.0. Other arguments pass through unchanged. It is a preset, not a separate layer class.

Zero clusters select uniform rotations; automatic spread is used only when clustering is active. See HuitEightLayer.

face.add_cube(spacing=0.5, radius=None, angle=0.0, hour=12, minute=0, distance=0.0, resolution=200, cuts_per_group=12, gap_per_group=6, amplitude=0.0, leg_angle=30.0) radius=None resolves to face.radius, defining the local clipping circle. angle rotates the pattern in radians; leg_angle is in degrees. amplitude=0.0 selects automatic amplitude. resolution is validated but does not control zigzag-vertex generation. The public wrapper defaults to 12 cuts and 6 gap spacings, whereas CubeLayer and the raw binding default to 8 and 8. An existing CubeLayer passed to add_cube_layer() or add() retains its own configuration.

GuillochePattern(radius) Creates an empty layer composition. radius is a read-only Python property in mm, with the same finite, inclusive 26–44 mm constraint as WatchFace. Combined SVG always adds the default dial circle, bezel, and 0.8 mm center-hole circle; this class has no Python methods to configure or disable them. The signatures below use pattern for a GuillochePattern instance. This section lists its exposed Python composition methods, not every public Rust method.

pattern.add_layer(spiro) pattern.add_flinque_layer(flinque) pattern.add_diamant_layer(diamant) pattern.add_limacon_layer(limacon) pattern.add_paon_layer(paon) add_layer(spiro) accepts only HorizontalSpirograph, VerticalSpirograph, or SphericalSpirograph. Other values raise TypeError. It reconstructs an origin-centered, ungenerated spirograph from its parameters. The other methods accept their corresponding standalone layer class and copy its configuration and center into a new, ungenerated internal layer. Their keyword parameter names are flinque, diamant, limacon, and paon, not layer. There is no generic add() method. Draperie, huit-eight, Clous de Paris, and Cube adders are not exposed on Python GuillochePattern, even though the Rust compositor supports them. WatchFace exposes those families.

Other strings raise ValueError. No whitespace stripping is performed. All base spirograph and positioning arguments are required. wave_amplitude and wave_frequency are used only for the vertical variant; dome_height is used only for the spherical variant. Unused options do not undergo that variant’s constructor checks, though Python-to-Rust type conversion still applies. Base parameter validation matches the standalone spirographs. All three spirographs use a hypotrochoid with fixed-circle radius outer_radius, rolling-circle radius outer_radius * radius_ratio, and pen offset point_distance * outer_radius * radius_ratio.
HorizontalSpirograph(outer_radius, radius_ratio, point_distance, rotations, resolution) Produces the planar hypotrochoid without additional modulation. All arguments are required.

VerticalSpirograph(outer_radius, radius_ratio, point_distance, rotations, resolution, wave_amplitude=1.0, wave_frequency=5.0) Adds wave_amplitude * sin(wave_frequency * t) to the planar curve’s y coordinate. wave_amplitude is in mm; wave_frequency is cycles per revolution of the curve parameter. “Vertical” refers to y modulation, not a z coordinate.

SphericalSpirograph(outer_radius, radius_ratio, point_distance, rotations, resolution, dome_height=5.0) Computes both the planar hypotrochoid and a spherical projection. dome_height is a positive length in mm. The projection derives sphere radius (outer_radius**2 + dome_height**2) / (2 * dome_height) and clamps the projection’s inverse-sine argument to its domain. Standalone SVG uses the planar points. Standalone STL and STEP use the projected 3D points. Composition uses the planar points even for combined STL and STEP; a spherical layer does not make a composed dial domed.

Values above 1 are allowed. rotations Positive integer number of parameter revolutions. resolution Positive integer samples per revolution. rotations * resolution Must not overflow and must be at most 1,000,000. wave_amplitude Vertical variant only: finite and nonnegative. wave_frequency Vertical variant only: finite; zero and negative values are accepted. dome_height Spherical variant only: finite and positive. Generation stores exactly rotations * resolution samples, without an additional endpoint sample. Curves need not return to their start. SVG does not forcibly close the path; standalone STL currently connects the final point back to the first. STEP exports the sampled polyline without adding that closing segment. Bit factories return a new CuttingBit. There is no public Python constructor. All dimensions below are in millimeters.

CuttingBit.v_shaped(angle, width): stores width. Clamps angle to 1–179 degrees, then computes depth = width / (2 * tan(angle_in_radians / 2)). CuttingBit.flat(width, depth): stores the supplied width and depth. CuttingBit.round(diameter): width = diameter, depth = diameter / 2. CuttingBit.elliptical(width, aspect_ratio): stores width; depth = width / (2 * aspect_ratio). aspect_ratio is the major-to-minor axis ratio. Clamping the V angle does not constitute general validation: widths, depths, diameters, and aspect ratios are not checked for positivity or finiteness. A zero elliptical aspect ratio can produce an infinite depth rather than a Python division exception. Lathe construction does not add bit validation.

width: read-only float; stored width or diameter in millimeters. depth: read-only float; stored or derived depth in millimeters. repr(bit) reports width and depth, not the bit shape. Shape access, custom profiles, cross sections, footprints, and Rust’s default bit are not exposed in Python.

RoseEngineLathe(config, bit), its with_center() factory, and the general RoseEngineLatheRun constructors validate the config when they copy it into a generator. They require: A finite, strictly positive base_radius. Finite, nonnegative primary and secondary amplitudes. Finite primary and secondary phases and start/end angles. resolution >= 10. These checks do not inspect rosette parameters, the bit, or depth-modulation parameters. Both config and bit are cloned during generator construction. RoseEngineLatheRun.flinque( radius=10.0, num_petals=12, num_waves=60, wave_amplitude=0.8, wave_frequency=20.0, inner_radius_ratio=0.05, center_x=0.0, center_y=0.0, ) Generates concentric chevron rings with fine radial ripple. num_passes == num_waves. Base ring radii use half-step positions uniformly between radius * inner_radius_ratio and radius. A ring is skipped when its base radius is less than 0.1 * wave_amplitude. num_petals is the chevron lobe count. Each retained ring has num_petals * 80 + 1 samples; there is no resolution argument. wave_amplitude is in millimeters. The radial addition is wave_amplitude * abs(sin(petal_phase)) plus a ripple of amplitude 0.05 * wave_amplitude and phase petal_phase * wave_frequency, where petal_phase = angle * num_petals / 2. Thus wave_frequency is a multiplier, and radius controls the base ring range rather than clipping the peaks. Construction checks positive ring count, finite positive radius, finite nonnegative half-amplitude, and finite centers. It does not check positive num_petals, the range of inner_radius_ratio, or finite wave_frequency. Zero petals can produce non-finite coordinates during generation.

RoseEngineLatheRun.huiteight( num_curves=72, scale=20.0, resolution=360, center_x=0.0, center_y=0.0, num_clusters=0, cluster_spread=0.0, ) Generates Cartesian lemniscates of Bernoulli through the pattern center. scale is the half-width in millimeters. num_passes == num_curves, and each curve has resolution + 1 samples. The spelling is huiteight(), unlike the rosette and config factories named huit_eight(); those radial factories do not generate this lemniscate. Uniform orientations span a half-turn, pi * i / num_curves, because a lemniscate has 180-degree rotational symmetry. Clustering is active only when 0 < num_clusters < num_curves. Curves are distributed evenly among clusters, with any remainder assigned to the earliest clusters. Cluster centers are separated by pi / num_clusters radians. A positive cluster_spread is the full angular span of each cluster; otherwise the span is automatically pi / (2 * num_clusters). Zero clusters, or a cluster count at least as large as the curve count, selects uniform orientations. Construction checks positive curve count, finite positive scale, and finite centers. RoseEngineLatheRun.clous_de_paris( spacing=1.0, radius=22.0, angle=0.7853981633974483, resolution=200, center_x=0.0, center_y=0.0, ) Generates two perpendicular sets of parallel straight lines clipped to a circle. spacing is perpendicular line spacing in millimeters; radius is the clipping radius in millimeters. angle rotates the grid in radians; its default is pi / 4 (45 degrees). Each line has resolution + 1 samples, including its circle-boundary endpoints. Tangent lines may contain coincident points. num_passes is always 1 for this preset, not the grid’s line count. Construction checks finite positive radius and finite centers. It does not validate spacing, angle, the requested resolution, or the derived line count. Finite positive spacing and a nonzero resolution are required for the generation formulas; zero or extremely small spacing can cause excessive iteration rather than an early ValueError.

Alternating groups shift by half a zigzag period. Lines are clipped geometrically to the circle of radius, then rotated by angle radians and translated to the supplied center.
